name: Roland TR-808
originalPurpose: A rhythm machine for musicians to practice and demo with, intended to sound like a drum kit.
whatActuallyHappened: It did not sound like a drum kit. It sounded like a machine, with a kick drum whose decay could be set so long it rang on like a bass note. It sold poorly, was discontinued after roughly three years, turned up cheap secondhand, and became the rhythmic foundation of electro, hip-hop, and a large share of pop music ever since.
priceStory: Around 1200 US dollars new in 1980, which was cheap next to a Linn LM-1 at close to 5000. After discontinuation it fell far enough that Bronx and Detroit producers could own one.
hook: A commercial failure that sounded wrong and therefore changed everything.
blurb: Roland wanted it to imitate a drum kit and it could not, so people stopped buying it. Its sounds were made by analogue circuits to save money, just before sampling real drums became affordable. But that long booming kick drum and that thin tick of a snare were sounds that did not exist before. Once it was cheap, the people who could afford it built new music on it, and the long kick has set what people expect from the low end of popular music for four decades. Its failure is the reason the story happened at all.
